metadata.title: Shannon Shakes Hands with Chernoff: Big Data Viewpoint On Channel Information Measures

nodes.name: Two data rules of the big data viewpoint
nodes.statement: Two data rules are believed. For one thing, the data does not lie. For other thing, we only need to guarantee that our conclusion is correct with very large probability rather than one in the era of big data [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}].

nodes.name: Nature of channel information conjecture (introduction)
nodes.statement: Based on these results, we put forward a conjecture that there is nature of channel information and no matter Shannon mutual information, Chernoff mutual information or other information measures, which are different measures of the same information quantity.
nodes.statement_short: All channel information measures (Shannon, Chernoff, others) measure one underlying 'nature of channel information'.
conclusions: there is nature of channel information
no matter Shannon mutual information, Chernoff mutual information or other information measures, which are different measures of the same information quantity

nodes.name: Mutual information
nodes.statement: The mutual information is a measure of the amount of information that one random variable contains about another variable. In fact, it describes the reduction in the uncertainty of one random variable if another one is known [\cite{Elements}].
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)
nodes.genus: a measure of the amount of information
differentia: that one random variable contains about another variable

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X,Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{x,y} {p(x,y)log{{p(x,y)} \over {p(x)p(y)}}} \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: Shannon mutual information $I_S(X,Y)$ is the KL divergence between the joint $p(x,y)$ and the product $p(x)p(y)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)
nodes.label: Shannon Information

nodes.name: Relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler distance)
nodes.statement: D(p||q) = \sum\limits_{x \in \textit{X}} {p(x)log{{p(x)} \over {q(x)}}}
nodes.statement_short: KL divergence $D(p||q)=\sum_x p(x)\log(p(x)/q(x))$.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)
nodes.label: KL distance

nodes.name: Chernoff information as optimal error exponent
nodes.statement: Chernoff Information is the resulting error exponent when minimizing the overall probability of error [\cite{Elements}].
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)
assumptions: when minimizing the overall probability of error
conclusions: Chernoff Information is the resulting error exponent

nodes.name: Chernoff information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} I_C({{\rm{P}}_1},{P_2}) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right) \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff information of $P_1,P_2$ is $-\min_{0\le\alpha\le1}\log\sum_x P_1^\alpha P_2^{1-\alpha}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)
nodes.label: Chernoff Information1

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} I_C(X,Y) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {\sum\limits_y {{p^\alpha }(x,y){{(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }}} } } \right). \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff mutual information: Chernoff information between the joint $p(x,y)$ and the product $p(x)p(y)$.
nodes.label: Chernoff Information2

nodes.name: Shannon vs Chernoff mutual information: different divergences
nodes.statement: In fact, both Shannon mutual information and Chernoff mutual information are to depict the inner relationship between two random variables. The difference is that they adopt different measures of the distance between two distributions. The relative entropy is adopted in Shannon mutual information and the R{\'{e}}nyi divergence is used in Chernoff mutual information [\cite{van2014renyi}].

nodes.name: Channel capacity
nodes.statement: the maximum mutual information is defined as the channel capacity for a discrete memoryless channel.
nodes.section: 2 Channel Information Measures and ACE Algorithm Description
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)

nodes.name: Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC)
nodes.statement: Consider the BSC, which is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelBSC}. It is a binary channel where the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$. The transmission error in it is $\varepsilon $.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)
differentia: the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$
The transmission error in it is $\varepsilon $

nodes.name: BSC Shannon mutual information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^2 {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^2 {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr & = (1 - \varepsilon )\log {{1 - \varepsilon } \over {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon }} + \varepsilon \log {\varepsilon \over {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )}}. \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: Closed form of Shannon mutual information of the BSC in terms of $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: BSC Mutual information

nodes.name: BSC Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ &=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log ( {(1 - \varepsilon )^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon } \right)^{1 - \alpha }} \\ &+ {\varepsilon ^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )} \right)^{1 - \alpha }} ) \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff mutual information of the BSC as a minimization over $\alpha$ in terms of $\lambda,\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: BSC Chernoff information

nodes.name: No explicit solution for BSC Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, there is no explicit solution for Eq.(\ref{BSC Chernoff information}). As a result, it is arduous to analyze the Chernoff mutual information.

nodes.name: Shannon and Chernoff mutual information seem different
nodes.statement: It is observed that the Shannon mutual information seems to be completely different from the Chernoff mutual information.

nodes.name: Multiple Symmetric Channel (MSC)
nodes.statement: The MSC is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelMBSC}. The number of input symbol is $M$. The probability of the input symbol is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...,\lambda_M)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+...+\lambda_M=1$ ($\lambda_i>0$).The transmission error of each one is $\frac{\varepsilon}{M-1}$.
differentia: The number of input symbol is $M$
The probability of the input symbol is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...,\lambda_M)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+...+\lambda_M=1$ ($\lambda_i>0$)
The transmission error of each one is $\frac{\varepsilon}{M-1}$

nodes.name: BSC is the special case of MSC for M=2
nodes.statement: The BSC is the special case of MSC for $M=2$.

nodes.name: MSC Shannon mutual information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^M {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^M {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: Shannon mutual information of the MSC as a double sum over the $M$ input and output symbols.
nodes.label: MSC Mutual information

nodes.name: MSC Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {{p(xy)}^\alpha (x){(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ \end{aligned}
nodes.label: MSC Chernoff information

nodes.name: Residual error of ACE
nodes.statement: Assume random variables $X_1,X_2,\cdots ,X_p$ are predictors and $Y$ is response. Supposing $\phi _1(X_1),\phi _2(X_2),\cdots,\phi _p(X_p),\theta (Y)$ are arbitrary zero mean functions of the corresponding variables, the residual error is \begin{equation} {e^2}\left( {\theta ,{\phi _1},\cdots,{\phi _p}} \right) = {{E\left\{ {{{\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right]}^2}} \right\}} \over {E\left[ {{\theta ^2}(Y)} \right]}} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: ACE residual error $e^2$: normalized mean-squared gap between $\theta(Y)$ and $\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)$.

nodes.name: ACE Algorithm (alternating conditional expectation)
nodes.statement: \caption{ACE Algorithm} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE set $\theta (Y) = Y/\left\| Y \right\|$ and ${\phi _1}({X_1}),...,{\phi _p}({X_p}) = 0$;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE For $k=1$ to p Do:\\ \begin{equation*} {\phi _{k,1}}({X_k}) = E\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i \ne k} {{\phi _i}\left( {{X_i}} \right)} \left| {{X_k}} \right.} \right]; \end{equation*} replace $\phi_k(X_k)$ with $\phi_{k,1}(X_k)$;\\ End For Loop;\\ \STATE End Inner Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE \begin{equation*} {\theta _1}(Y) = {{E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1} {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \over {\left\| {E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \right\|}}; \end{equation*} replace $\theta(Y)$ with $\theta_1(Y)$;\\ \STATE End Outer Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE $\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p$ are the solution $\theta^*,\phi^*_1,...,\phi^*_p$;\\ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Alternating conditional expectations: update each $\phi_k$ then $\theta$ by conditional expectations until $e^2$ stops decreasing.
nodes.label: alg:ACE

nodes.name: Channel information as a function of channel parameters
nodes.label: Eq ACE Alg4

nodes.name: ACE precondition: known independent parameters and known f
nodes.statement: It is supposed that ${X_1},{X_2},...,{X_p}$ are known and independent. Moreover, the functional relation $f$ is also known since it is defined by human to describe the channel information.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition of channel information
nodes.statement: \theta (Y) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}(X_i)} + \delta
nodes.statement_short: ACE yields $\theta(Y)=\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)+\delta$, separating each channel parameter's effect.
nodes.label: ACE_Def

nodes.name: Simulation Procedure
nodes.statement: \caption*{Simulation Procedure} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE Generate channel parameters, such as $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$; \STATE Calculate the channel information measures, such as Shannon mutual information; \STATE Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm; \STATE Repeat above process till the required times. \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Monte Carlo loop: sample channel parameters, compute information measures, decompose them with ACE, repeat.
nodes.label: alg:simulated

nodes.name: Simulated example: BSC
nodes.statement: $20000$ observations geneated from the Eq.(\ref{BSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{BSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$ are independently drawn from a uniform distribution $U(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with two input parameters.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition of BSC data is excellent
nodes.statement: The ACE algorithm is applied to this simulated data set and the results is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I}. The correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda)+\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is extremely close to $1$. Furthermore, The error of the ACE decomposition $\delta$ is invariably near to zero. Clearly, both of them have shown that the ACE decomposition results are excellent.
assumptions: The ACE algorithm is applied to this simulated data set
conclusions: The correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda)+\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is extremely close to $1$
The error of the ACE decomposition $\delta$ is invariably near to zero
the ACE decomposition results are excellent

nodes.name: BSC: Shannon and Chernoff ACE transformations coincide
nodes.statement: It is noted that function curve of $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ w.r.t. Shannon mutual information is almost coincided with that w.r.t Chernoff mutual information after the ACE decomposition. As a result, in the range of the errors permitted, the $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ appears to be coincided with each other. $\phi_1(\lambda)$ is monotone decreasing function. The greater $\lambda$, the faster the decline in $\phi_1(\lambda)$. Furthermore, $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is symmetric around the line $\varepsilon = 0.5$ for the fact that the channel is symmetrical about $\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: For the BSC, ACE gives nearly identical $\phi_1(\lambda),\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ for Shannon and Chernoff; $\phi_1$ decreasing, $\phi_2$ symmetric about 0.5.
assumptions: $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$ are independently drawn from a uniform distribution $U(0,1)$
conclusions: function curve of $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ w.r.t. Shannon mutual information is almost coincided with that w.r.t Chernoff mutual information after the ACE decomposition
$\phi_1(\lambda)$ is monotone decreasing function
$\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is symmetric around the line $\varepsilon = 0.5$

nodes.statement: The results of Shannon mutual information are smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole variant trend is identical. $\theta(y)$ increases rapidly when $y$ is close to zero and the slope of its curve is becoming smaller as $y$ increases.
assumptions: $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$ are independently drawn from a uniform distribution $U(0,1)$
conclusions: The results of Shannon mutual information are smaller than the Chernoff mutual information
whole variant trend is identical

nodes.name: Simulated example: MSC
nodes.statement: $60000$ observations generated from the Eq.(\ref{MSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{MSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. They are generated randomly and independently, which is bound in $(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with four input parameters.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition of MSC data is valid
nodes.statement: Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I} shows similar characteristics that in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I}. The value of the ACE decomposition error $\delta$ is still very small. On the other hand, the correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda_1)+\phi_2(\lambda_2)+\phi_3(\lambda_3)+\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is close to $1$. These two points verify the validity of the ACE algorithm again.
assumptions: They are generated randomly and independently, which is bound in $(0,1)$
conclusions: The value of the ACE decomposition error $\delta$ is still very small
the correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda_1)+\phi_2(\lambda_2)+\phi_3(\lambda_3)+\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is close to $1$

nodes.name: MSC: Shannon and Chernoff ACE transformations coincide
nodes.statement: It is obviously that the function curves of $\theta(y)$,$\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$,$\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ and $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ are almost the same for these two channel information measures. It is worth noting that the minimum of $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ occurs when $\varepsilon \approx 0.75$. The values of $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is big when $\varepsilon$ is very close to $0$ or $1$. Moreover, $\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$ and $\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ are very similar. Their function curve is flat and close to zero when the independent variable (the probability of the input symbol) is less than $0.7$ . When the independent variable approaches to $1$, the values of them rapid decrease. In fact, it is reasonable because these input variables are equivalent for the channel.
nodes.statement_short: For the MSC, ACE transformations are nearly identical for Shannon and Chernoff; $\phi_4$ minimal near $\varepsilon\approx0.75$.
assumptions: They are generated randomly and independently, which is bound in $(0,1)$
conclusions: the function curves of $\theta(y)$,$\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$,$\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ and $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ are almost the same for these two channel information measures
the minimum of $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ occurs when $\varepsilon \approx 0.75$
$\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$ and $\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ are very similar

nodes.name: Probably approximately correct (PAC) model
nodes.statement: In fact, the probably approximately correct (PAC) model is enough for us in most of time [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}]. In this model, one only need to construct algorithms which guarantee that it is correct with high probability (not necessarily one). This model is the foundation of Support Vector Machine (SVM) [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}].

nodes.name: ACE result as compound function
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} Y = f\left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \overset{(a)}{=}{\theta ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right)= \psi \left( {\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} \right)\\ \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: Ignoring residual $\delta$, $Y=\theta^{-1}(\sum_i\phi_i(X_i))=\psi(\varphi(\mathbf{X}))$.
nodes.label: Res_Fun

nodes.name: Shannon and Chernoff differ only in the outer function
nodes.statement: From the figures above, it is noted that $ \phi_i(X_i)$ is almost the same for both Shannon and Chernoff mutual information. For these two measures, the only difference is $\theta(\cdot)$. The function $\psi(\cdot)$ is different and ${\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} $ is the same.
nodes.statement_short: The inner functions $\phi_i$ (hence $\varphi(\mathbf X)$) agree for Shannon and Chernoff; only $\theta$ (hence $\psi$) differs.
assumptions: $Y$ is the channel information and ${\textbf{X}}$ is all the set of all the input channel parameters
conclusions: $ \phi_i(X_i)$ is almost the same for both Shannon and Chernoff mutual information
For these two measures, the only difference is $\theta(\cdot)$
The function $\psi(\cdot)$ is different and ${\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} $ is the same

nodes.name: Shannon's inverse transformation exceeds Chernoff's
nodes.statement: From the Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I} to Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I}, it is also noted that the function $\theta(\cdot)$ is monotonic function. As mentioned above, the curves of $\theta(\cdot)$ have the same trend and the values of $\theta(Y)$ for Shannon mutual information is invariably smaller than those for Chernoff information. Therefore, the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\theta$ is monotone and Shannon's $\theta(Y)$ is always smaller, Shannon's $\theta^{-1}$ exceeds Chernoff's.
assumptions: the values of $\theta(Y)$ for Shannon mutual information is invariably smaller than those for Chernoff information
conclusions: the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's

nodes.name: Kullback-Leibler divergence as special case of Rényi divergence
nodes.statement: Over the last decades, Shannon information and Chernoff information are always considered to be two kinds of channel information measures and the relation between them is that Kullback-Leibler divergence is the special case of R{\'{e}}nyi divergence when $\alpha=1$.

nodes.name: Shannon Shakes Hands with Chernoff
nodes.statement: However, with the aid of the ACE algorithm, we find the inner relations between them. In fact, they are different metrics of the same physical quantity. For a channel, in a certain time, if all of its parameters are given, all of its state and properties will be determined. Thus the information about the same channel is always consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Shannon and Chernoff mutual information are different metrics of the same physical quantity of channel information.
assumptions: if all of its parameters are given
conclusions: they are different metrics of the same physical quantity
all of its state and properties will be determined
the information about the same channel is always consistent

nodes.name: Channel parameters decide the nature of channel
nodes.statement: Obviously, the ability to convey information of a channel is decided by input parameters. That is to say, the parameters represent the channel. As a result, we hold opinion that these channel parameters decide the nature of channel.

nodes.name: Nature of channel information
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \varPsi=\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: The nature of channel information $\varPsi$ is the inner function $\varphi(\mathbf X)$ of the channel parameters.
nodes.label: Nature_Fun

nodes.name: Channel information measure as function of the nature
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \rm{I}= \psi (\varPsi) \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Nature_Fun1

nodes.name: Conjecture on decomposition of novel information measures
nodes.statement: There is a conjecture that if a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information, it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent.
nodes.statement_short: Any new channel information measure decomposes under ACE as some outer function $\psi$ of the common nature $\varPsi$.
assumptions: a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information
conclusions: it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent

nodes.name: Using the conjecture to judge and construct information measures
nodes.statement: This rule can be used to judge the rationality of the new information measure. This conjecture also provides a way for us to propose a new information measure for the fact that we can construct that based on designing the function $\psi(\cdot)$. In fact, even if this guess is not right with probability one, the new one which conforms to the law is correct with large probability and we can easily find the relation between that and previous information measures, such as Shannon and Chernoff information.
